options: Defined, published criteria for each color tied to measurable thresholds, so a red means the same thing every month
Assigning colors based on how the CISO feels that morning
Never using red to avoid difficult conversations
Changing the thresholds each month to keep everything green
explain: RAG only works with objective, stable criteria — without defined thresholds it becomes mood art that leadership learns to ignore. Feeling-based colors, red-avoidance, and shifting goalposts all convert the report from a governance tool into theater.

q: A dashboard tracks both 'percentage of critical patches applied within SLA' and 'number of new ransomware variants observed in the wild.' Which is the KPI and which is the KRI?
options: Both are KRIs
Patch SLA compliance is the KPI (it measures our performance); emerging ransomware variants are a KRI (they signal changing risk in the environment)
The distinction does not matter for reporting
Both are KPIs
explain: KPIs measure how well we execute (patch performance is within our control); KRIs signal shifts in the risk landscape (threat trends are not). Conflating them misleads leadership about what management can actually influence, and the distinction is exactly what makes dashboards interpretable.

q: An incident report marked TLP:RED contains sensitive victim details. A partner organization asks for a copy to check their own exposure. What is the correct handling?
options: Send it — sharing is always good
Post a summary publicly so everyone can check
Decline or sanitize: TLP:RED restricts distribution to named recipients only, so share only with explicit originator approval or provide a sanitized version at a lower TLP level
Forward it to the partner's entire mailing list
explain: TLP:RED means eyes-only for named recipients — honoring it may require declining, seeking originator approval, or producing a sanitized TLP:AMBER/GREEN version. Unrestricted sharing violates the marking and the trust behind it, public posting is the worst possible handling, and mailing-list forwarding multiplies the violation.

q: The vulnerability team proudly reports '1,200 tickets closed this quarter' as proof of progress. Why might leadership be right to question this metric?
options: Leadership should never question security metrics
More closed tickets always means less risk
Ticket counts are always accurate
Closed tickets can reflect reassignment, deduplication, or risk acceptance rather than actual remediation — report verified fix rates and rescanned closure instead
explain: Closure is a workflow event, not a risk outcome — tickets close for administrative reasons constantly, so verified remediation (rescanned clean) is the honest measure. Treating all closures as fixes inflates progress, leadership questioning metrics is healthy governance, and volume alone says nothing about residual risk.

q: An external audit produces 15 findings. What tracking structure BEST ensures they actually get remediated?
options: Named owner, agreed remediation plan, due date, and independent retesting for each finding, reported regularly until closure
Assigning all findings to the intern
Waiting for the next audit to check
A spreadsheet nobody opens after the audit
explain: Findings close through accountability: an owner, a plan, a deadline, and verification that the fix worked — reported until done. Forgotten spreadsheets, joke assignments, and waiting a year for the next audit are how findings become repeat findings.

q: The company deployed EDR to 100% of endpoints. In the quarterly report, what BEST demonstrates the control is actually effective?
options: The deployment percentage — coverage equals effectiveness
Test results: detection rates against simulated attack techniques, mean time to detect and respond, and coverage of ATT&CK techniques — proving the control works, not just that it exists
The vendor's marketing claims
The amount spent on licenses
explain: Effectiveness is proven by testing outcomes — simulated attacks caught, detection speed, technique coverage — not by installation counts. Deployment percentage measures rollout, vendor claims measure marketing, and spend measures budget; none of them show the control stopping anything.

q: The incident report's timeline section lists events with timestamps from five different log sources. What is the MOST important quality control for this section?
options: Making the timeline as long as possible
Verifying timestamp accuracy and timezone normalization across sources, and clearly marking which events are confirmed versus inferred
Using only one log source for simplicity
Writing the timeline before the investigation finishes
explain: A timeline is only as trustworthy as its timestamps — unnormalized timezones and mixed confirmed/inferred events produce false sequences that mislead every downstream decision. Length is not quality, single-source timelines miss the full picture, and premature timelines enshrine guesses as fact.

q: After-action items from three incidents are all assigned to 'the security team' generally, and none are complete. What is the root cause of the follow-through failure?
options: After-action items are optional
Incidents should not be reviewed
The team is lazy
No named individual owner with a due date — collective assignment means no one is accountable, so items drift
explain: Accountability requires a name and a date — 'the team' owns nothing, so nothing gets done; this is the most common lessons-learned failure mode. Blaming character misses the structural cause, action items are commitments not suggestions, and skipping reviews guarantees repeated mistakes.

q: The SOC builds one dashboard for analysts and one for executives from the same data. What is the key design difference?
options: The executive dashboard emphasizes trends, risk posture, and business impact with plain language; the analyst dashboard shows granular, real-time operational detail
Executives get more technical detail than analysts
Dashboards should only show green metrics
There should be no difference — one dashboard for everyone
explain: Audience-appropriate design: executives decide from trends and risk posture in business language, analysts operate from real-time granularity. One-size dashboards serve neither, inverting the detail level confuses both audiences, and green-only dashboards are propaganda.

q: Quarterly phishing click rates were 12%, 9%, 11%, and 4%. How should this be reported to show the real story?
options: Report only the 4% — the latest number is all that matters
Show the trend across all four quarters with context on what changed (new training, reporting button) — the downward direction with one anomaly quarter tells the improvement story honestly
Average them to 9% and report a single number
Report the 12% to justify more budget
explain: Trends with context show trajectory and credibility — the 11% quarter invites honest explanation rather than hiding. Cherry-picking the best quarter misleads, a bare average erases the improvement story, and leading with the worst number for budget is manipulation that destroys trust when discovered.

q: A peer company reports 99.9% patch compliance in 7 days. Your CISO wants to benchmark against them. What caution applies?
options: Publicly dispute their numbers
Benchmarking is always valid — copy their target immediately
Peer numbers lack context: different asset mixes, scope definitions, and measurement methods make direct comparison misleading — use benchmarks as directional input, not binding targets
Refuse to measure anything peers measure
explain: Benchmarks without methodology context compare apples to oranges — scope, asset criticality, and definitions vary wildly, so they inform but do not dictate targets. Blind copying imports someone else's context, refusing measurement surrenders insight, and public disputes burn industry relationships.

q: How often should the CISO brief the board on cybersecurity, and what should drive the cadence?
options: Daily — the board needs every detail
Never — boards do not care about security
Only after a breach
Quarterly, aligned to the board's existing risk-governance rhythm — with ad-hoc briefings for material incidents, so security becomes routine oversight rather than crisis theater
explain: Regular quarterly cadence normalizes security as governance while reserving ad-hoc sessions for genuinely material events. Breach-only briefings train the board to associate security with failure, daily briefings drown governance in noise, and 'never' abdicates the CISO's reporting duty.

q: An incident report contains customer PII and internal network diagrams. It must go to the cyber insurer. What handling is required?
options: Classify and mark the document, encrypt it in transit, limit distribution to need-to-know recipients, and confirm the insurer's secure intake channel
Post it to the insurer's public support forum
Remove all useful detail before sending
Send it unmarked over regular email
explain: Sensitive reports need the full handling chain: classification markings, encrypted transmission, minimal distribution, and verified secure receipt. Unmarked email exposes PII in transit, public forums are a breach in themselves, and gutting the detail defeats the report's purpose.

q: Legal counsel asks that incident investigation notes be prepared to preserve attorney-client privilege. What does this practically require of the security team?
options: Marking documents as privileged makes them privileged regardless of process

Working at counsel's direction, limiting distribution to those with a need to know, and segregating privileged investigation materials from ordinary business records — privilege depends on process, not labels
Deleting all notes after the incident
Nothing changes — privilege is automatic
explain: Privilege is earned through process: counsel-directed work product, tight need-to-know distribution, and separation from routine records. It is never automatic, labels alone do not create it, and deleting notes is spoliation that destroys both the investigation and any privilege claim.

q: The after-action report lists 12 improvements. What structure BEST ensures they survive beyond the report?
options: Filing the report where auditors can find it
A hopeful closing paragraph
Each improvement gets a named owner, a due date, and a tracking entry reviewed at a set cadence until verified complete
Assigning all 12 to the CISO personally
explain: Improvements die without accountability mechanics — owner, date, tracked review, verified completion. Hope is not a control, loading everything on one executive guarantees bottleneck failure, and audit-findability is not implementation.

q: The SOC reports 'mean time to contain' of 4 hours, but one 72-hour outlier skewed the average while most incidents contained in under 1 hour. What is the honest way to report this?
options: Delete the outlier from the data
Stop reporting containment time
Report only the mean — 4 hours is the number
Report the median alongside the mean and explain the outlier, so leadership sees typical performance versus the average
explain: Median plus mean with outlier context tells the truth: typical performance was under an hour, one severe case pulled the average. Mean-only reporting misrepresents the norm, deleting data is dishonest, and abandoning the metric loses visibility into real performance.

q: The board approved a formal risk acceptance for an unpatched legacy system last year. What must the CISO report this year?
options: The acceptance's current status: whether conditions changed, whether compensating controls still hold, and a recommendation to renew, remediate, or retire — risk acceptance is a living decision, not a one-time pass
A request to delete the original acceptance
Only good news about the system
Nothing — the board already approved it
explain: Risk acceptances require periodic re-presentation: threat landscape, control effectiveness, and business need all shift, so the board must re-decide with fresh facts. 'Already approved' treats acceptance as permanent, deleting records breaks governance, and good-news-only reporting hides the actual risk position.

q: A proposed $120,000 network segmentation project would reduce the expected annual breach loss from $500,000 to $150,000. How should this be presented to justify the spend?
options: 'Trust us, it is important'
Cost-benefit in risk terms: $350,000 in expected annual loss reduction against $120,000 cost — a clear positive return on security investment
Only the technical architecture diagram
A promise that breaches will never happen
explain: Security spend is justified by risk economics: quantified loss reduction versus cost gives leadership a business decision, not a technical plea. 'Trust us' is not analysis, architecture diagrams do not show value, and promising zero breaches guarantees a credibility loss at the next incident.

q: The incident communication plan names who declares an incident, who notifies legal, and who speaks to the press. What framework concept does this assignment of responsibilities represent?
options: A firewall rule
A risk heat map
A RACI matrix — defining who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each communication action, so nothing falls through cracks during a crisis
A vulnerability scan schedule
explain: RACI eliminates crisis confusion by pre-assigning decision rights and communication duties — during an incident there is no time to debate who calls legal. Firewall rules, heat maps, and scan schedules are unrelated artifacts that do not assign human responsibility.

q: Legal requires incident reports retained for 7 years, but IT's default retention deletes them after 1 year. What is the correct resolution?
options: Delete everything immediately to reduce liability
Keep reports forever with no schedule
Follow IT's default — simpler
Apply the longer legal retention requirement to incident reports, document the retention schedule, and implement a legal-hold override process for active matters
explain: Legal and regulatory requirements override operational defaults: the retention schedule must reflect the 7-year duty with documented holds for active cases. Defaulting to 1 year invites sanctions, mass deletion is spoliation, and indefinite retention without a schedule creates its own discovery and privacy burdens.

q: During a threat hunt you query domain controller Security logs for Event ID 4769 (Kerberos service ticket requested). You find a standard user account requesting service tickets for dozens of service principal names (MSSQLSvc, HTTP, TERMSRV) in rapid succession, all using RC4-HMAC encryption, from a single workstation. No administrator was running a scan. What does this indicate, and what is the BEST response?
options: Likely Kerberoasting: the attacker is harvesting crackable service tickets to brute-force service account passwords offline. Investigate the source host and reset the affected service account passwords to long random values (or move them to managed service accounts).
Normal Kerberos behavior: service ticket requests are routine and RC4 is the default encryption type, so no action is needed.
AS-REP roasting: disable Kerberos pre-authentication on the affected accounts to stop it.
A firewall problem: block TCP/UDP port 88 between workstations and domain controllers to stop the ticket requests.
explain: Bulk TGS requests for many SPNs with RC4 encryption is the Kerberoasting pattern: RC4-encrypted tickets can be cracked offline, so the fix is investigating the source and rotating service account passwords to long, random values (gMSAs eliminate the problem). It is not normal behavior at this volume and encryption type; disabling pre-authentication addresses AS-REP roasting, a different attack against 4768 events; and blocking port 88 would break Kerberos authentication entirely.

q: Your NDR flags a workstation making hundreds of Netlogon RPC authentication attempts against a domain controller, each failing and immediately retrying with a modified authenticator, over several minutes. The DC System log shows Event ID 5829 entries noting vulnerable Netlogon secure channel connections. What is the MOST likely attack?
options: Normal domain replication traffic between the workstation and the domain controller.

ZeroLogon (CVE-2020-1472): exploitation of the Netlogon cryptographic flaw to escalate to domain admin. Verify the DC is patched and enforcing secure channel, and check for anomalous DC password changes.
Password spraying: the attacker is guessing passwords against the domain controller.
DCSync: the attacker is replicating directory data via Directory Replication Service RPC.
explain: Rapid-fire Netlogon authenticator retries plus Event ID 5829 (vulnerable secure channel allowed) is the ZeroLogon signature: the AES-CFB8 flaw lets an attacker spoof the DC's machine account. Password spraying guesses credentials rather than hammering Netlogon crypto; DCSync uses DRS RPC calls, not Netlogon authenticator retries; and legitimate replication never looks like hundreds of failed authenticator attempts.

q: Forensics on a compromised workstation shows the attacker coerced authentication from a server using an EFS RPC call, relayed the captured NTLM authentication to the enterprise certificate authority web enrollment endpoint, and obtained a certificate for a Domain Admin account. Which misconfiguration made this possible, and what is the BEST remediation?
options: The EFS Remote Protocol should be disabled on every server in the domain to stop coercion.
Shorten the validity period of all issued certificates to 24 hours.

AD CS web enrollment accepted NTLM authentication without relay protections (ESC8). Enable Extended Protection for Authentication on the CA web services, require Kerberos-only authentication, and disable NTLM for enrollment endpoints.
The CA issued too many certificates, so reduce the issuance quota.
explain: This is ESC8: NTLM relay to AD CS HTTP enrollment, which succeeds when the enrollment endpoints accept NTLM without Extended Protection. The durable fix is EPA plus Kerberos-only on CES/CEP. Disabling one coercion vector (EFS RPC/PetitPotam) is whack-a-mole since many coercion methods exist; issuance quotas and shorter lifetimes do nothing to stop fraudulent issuance.

q: You need reliable detection whenever any user runs common living-off-the-land downloaders (curl, wget, python3 one-liners) on 2,000 Linux servers, capturing the full command line and the invoking user, without deploying a commercial EDR. Which native control BEST meets this need?
options: Parse /var/log/messages for downloader activity.
Run a cron job every minute that snapshots ps output on each server.
Rely on each user's bash history file.

Linux auditd with execve syscall rules (for example, -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve), forwarding audit logs to the SIEM: every process execution is captured at the kernel with UID and arguments.
explain: auditd hooks the execve syscall in the kernel, so every execution is logged with the real UID and full arguments regardless of how the binary was invoked. /var/log/messages does not record process execution; minute-interval ps snapshots miss short-lived processes; and bash history is per-user, trivially disabled (unset HISTFILE) or deleted by an attacker.

q: Threat intel describes a new Linux rootkit. You want to hunt fleet-wide for its indicators: a hidden kernel module name, a specific listening port, and a modified /etc/ld.so.preload, correlated in a single pass. The fleet already runs an agent that supports SQL-based host interrogation. Which approach fits BEST?
options: osquery: write one SQL query joining the kernel_modules, listening_ports, and file tables and run it across the fleet, correlating all three indicators per host in a single result set.
Run an Nmap scan of the fleet to find the listening port.
SSH into each host in a loop and grep for the indicators.
Review NetFlow records for the listening port.
explain: osquery exposes OS state as SQL tables, so one query can join kernel modules, listening ports, and file contents per host across the fleet. Nmap only reveals the port with no host-artifact context; SSH loops do not scale and cannot join data structurally; NetFlow shows traffic, not kernel modules or preload files.

q: Your NDR team wants to fingerprint SSH client implementations to spot non-standard tools (custom implants, Paramiko-based C2) regardless of destination IP or port. JA3 does not apply because the traffic is SSH, not TLS. Which technique fits?
options: SSH banner grabbing on all outbound connections.
HASSH: hash the SSH handshake (key exchange algorithms, ciphers, and client version string) to fingerprint client implementations, then alert on rare or unknown HASSH values in the environment.
JA3 fingerprinting of the SSH handshake.
Block outbound TCP port 22 at the perimeter firewall.
explain: HASSH is the SSH analogue of JA3: it fingerprints the KEXINIT parameters and client string, exposing toolkits like Paramiko even on nonstandard ports. JA3 requires a TLS ClientHello and cannot fingerprint SSH; blocking port 22 breaks legitimate administration while implants simply use port 443; and banners are trivially spoofed strings, not cryptographic fingerprints.

q: Your detection engineers need three rules: (1) match a distinctive byte pattern in malware samples on disk, (2) alert on suspicious Windows process-creation telemetry in the SIEM, (3) alert on malicious traffic patterns at the NIDS. Which rule-language assignment is CORRECT?
options: YARA for the network traffic patterns and Snort for the malware samples.
Snort rules for the Windows event logs and YARA for the SIEM telemetry.
YARA for the malware byte patterns, Sigma for the SIEM process-creation telemetry, Snort/Suricata rules for the NIDS traffic patterns.
Sigma for all three, since it is vendor-neutral.
explain: Each language targets a data type: YARA matches byte patterns in files and memory, Sigma expresses log/telemetry detections portably across SIEMs, and Snort/Suricata inspects network packets. Sigma cannot match raw file bytes or packets; YARA does not parse packets; Snort does not read Windows event logs.

q: Monitoring shows traffic destined for your company's /24 suddenly routed through an autonomous system in another country that never announced your prefix before, coinciding with user reports of certificate warnings on the customer portal. What is the MOST likely cause, and what is the BEST detective control?
options: DNS cache poisoning: flush the resolver caches.
Normal anycast routing: anycast routinely shifts traffic between regions.
A misconfigured perimeter firewall rule.
BGP prefix hijack: an unauthorized AS is announcing your prefix to intercept traffic. Deploy RPKI route-origin authorizations and BGP monitoring that alerts on unauthorized origin AS announcements.
explain: A new foreign origin AS for your prefix plus interception symptoms (certificate warnings) is the BGP hijack pattern; RPKI ROAs let the world validate legitimate origins and BGP monitoring detects rogue announcements. DNS poisoning affects name resolution, not global routing; legitimate anycast is authorized and would not trigger certificate warnings; firewalls do not change global BGP announcements.

q: Brand monitoring flags a newly registered domain that renders identically to your company's domain in most browsers but substitutes Cyrillic characters for Latin ones (for example, Cyrillic 'a' U+0430). A certificate was issued for it within hours. What is this technique, and what is the BEST defensive action?
options: IDN homograph attack: visually identical confusable glyphs via internationalized domain names. Monitor certificate transparency logs for punycode (xn--) variants, block at the gateway, pursue takedown, and warn staff.
Typosquatting: register the misspelled variants yourself.
Subdomain takeover: reclaim the dangling DNS record.
No action needed: all browsers display punycode, so users cannot be fooled.
explain: Homograph attacks use Unicode confusables that render identically to the legitimate domain; punycode (xn--) appears in CT logs and raw URLs for detection. Typosquatting relies on misspellings, a different technique; there is no dangling DNS here, so takeover does not apply; and browser punycode display is inconsistent (many render Unicode when the label is single-script), so it cannot be relied upon.

q: An older runbook says to mark public threat reports 'TLP:WHITE'. A new FIRST standard renamed this marking. An analyst asks whether old TLP:WHITE reports must be relabeled and whether recipients' handling obligations changed. What is the correct guidance?
options: The rename only applies to government reports; keep using TLP:WHITE internally.
TLP:WHITE was renamed TLP:CLEAR with identical handling (no distribution restrictions). No relabeling is required and obligations are unchanged; update templates going forward.
TLP:WHITE now means restricted distribution, so recall and relabel all old reports immediately.
TLP:CLEAR requires a signed NDA before sharing.
explain: FIRST's TLP 2.0 renamed WHITE to CLEAR purely for clarity; the semantics (unlimited distribution) are unchanged, so retroactive relabeling is unnecessary churn. It did not become restricted, it does not require an NDA, and the rename applies to the standard itself, not just government use.

q: Your team shares STIX 2.1 threat intel with three partner organizations. Emailing STIX JSON bundles is error-prone and partners poll a shared folder manually. Which standard protocol is DESIGNED for automated STIX sharing, and what does it provide?
options: PGP-encrypted email with STIX attachments on a schedule.
SNMP traps carrying the indicators.
TAXII: an HTTPS-based sharing protocol with servers hosting collections (and channels) of STIX 2.x objects, supporting automated poll/push exchange with access control.
Syslog over TLS: forward the STIX bundles as log messages.
explain: TAXII is the purpose-built transport for STIX 2.x: TAXII servers expose collections that clients automatically poll or receive pushes from, with proper access control. Syslog is a log transport without intel semantics; scheduled email remains manual and brittle; SNMP is for network device management, not threat-intel exchange.

q: Leadership tells the intel team to 'watch everything.' Analysts are drowning in feeds and producing nothing decision-makers use. Which practice BEST focuses collection on what matters?
options: Subscribe to additional commercial threat feeds for broader coverage.
Automatically block every IOC from every feed at the perimeter.
Write longer, more detailed monthly threat reports.
Define Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs) with stakeholders, such as whether ransomware affiliates are targeting the sector this quarter, and drive collection and dissemination against them.
explain: PIRs tie intelligence work to decisions leadership actually faces, focusing collection instead of boiling the ocean. More feeds worsen overload; auto-blocking is an operational control action, not an intel-focusing practice; and longer reports increase volume without improving relevance.

q: You deploy a new Sigma rule for credential dumping. Before trusting it in production, you want to safely execute the adversary technique in a lab and confirm the rule fires with the expected fields. Which framework is DESIGNED for this validation?
options: Atomic Red Team: small, MITRE ATT&CK-mapped atomic tests designed to be executed safely to validate that detections fire as expected.
A full red team engagement against the production environment.
A vulnerability scan of the lab systems.
A discussion-based tabletop exercise with the SOC.
explain: Atomic Red Team provides discrete, ATT&CK-mapped technique tests ideal for per-rule detection validation in a lab. Full red teams are campaign-level and heavyweight; vulnerability scans find weaknesses but do not execute adversary techniques; tabletops are discussion-based with no execution at all.

q: An infected host exfiltrated 40 GB over HTTPS to a newly registered external IP. The firewall allows all outbound traffic by default, and the business legitimately needs web, email, and SaaS. What is the MOST effective architectural control to limit the NEXT exfiltration?
options: Install additional antivirus agents on all workstations.
Default-deny egress filtering with allowlisted destinations and ports, fronted by a TLS-inspecting proxy: new or unknown destinations are blocked or alerted instead of freely reachable.
Block outbound TCP port 443 at the perimeter firewall.
Improve incident response speed so the next exfiltration is caught sooner.
explain: Egress filtering with default-deny constrains where internal hosts can reach, breaking both C2 and bulk exfiltration paths while the proxy maintains business web access. Blocking 443 outright breaks the business; faster IR is detective rather than preventive; and antivirus already failed to stop the initial infection.

q: Attackers keep reaching newly registered malicious domains faster than your blocklists update: resolution happens before any feed has rated the domain. Which control BEST closes this gap?
options: Disable DNS resolution for workstations.
Add entries to each workstation's hosts file.

Protective DNS (DNS firewall / Response Policy Zones): enforce policy at resolution time using threat intel plus heuristics such as newly-observed-domain aging, sinkholing malicious lookups before connections occur.
Distribute blocklist updates by email more frequently.
explain: Protective DNS acts at resolution time with intel and new-domain heuristics, catching threats blocklists have not yet rated. Faster emails are still reactive; disabling DNS breaks all connectivity; hosts files do not scale and cannot apply dynamic policy.

q: You need intrusion detection for the OT network running the plant, but an active scan crashed a PLC last year and safety engineering rejects any inline device as an availability risk. Which monitoring approach fits?
options: Aggressive scheduled vulnerability scans of the OT network.
An inline intrusion prevention system in blocking mode.
Install host-based agents on the PLCs.
Passive network monitoring via TAP/SPAN with OT-protocol-aware analysis (Modbus, DNP3 parsing): full visibility with zero injected packets and no inline failure point.
explain: OT demands passive, protocol-aware monitoring: TAP/SPAN copies see everything without touching fragile devices or sitting in the path. Active scanning already proved dangerous to PLCs; inline IPS introduces the exact availability risk safety rejected; and proprietary controllers cannot run host agents.

q: Customers report a social media profile using your CEO's name and photo, DMing them fraudulent 'investment opportunities.' No corporate systems are compromised. What is the BEST response?
options: Report the profile through the platform's impersonation channels, preserve evidence, warn customers and staff publicly, and monitor for copycats: this is external brand abuse, not an endpoint compromise.
Isolate the CEO's laptop and begin forensic imaging.
Force a password reset for the CEO's corporate accounts.
Ignore it: with no systems compromised, it is not a security matter.
explain: External impersonation is handled via platform abuse reports, evidence preservation, and proactive customer/staff warnings; there is no compromised host to isolate. Imaging the laptop and resetting passwords respond to a compromise that the facts do not support, while ignoring it abandons defrauded customers and the brand.

q: After several MFA fatigue incidents, where attackers spammed push approvals until a tired user tapped 'Approve,' which control BEST mitigates this specific technique while keeping push-based MFA?
options: Require longer, more complex passwords.
Number matching: the user must enter the number displayed on the login screen into the authenticator app, so blindly approving a push no longer grants access.
Send additional push notifications to confirm intent.
Replace push MFA with SMS one-time codes.
explain: Number matching binds the approval to the specific login session shown on screen, defeating blind approval. More pushes worsen fatigue; SMS codes are weaker (SIM-swap and phishing); password complexity is orthogonal to push-approval abuse.

q: You need DLP to catch customer SSNs and account numbers even when slightly altered, but regexes alone flood the SOC with false positives on any 9-digit number. Which DLP technique BEST balances precision and coverage?
options: Block all outbound file uploads at the proxy.
Write more specific regular expressions.
Exact Data Matching (EDM): fingerprint the actual sensitive database records and match content against the fingerprint index, catching excerpts and alterations with low false positives.
Keyword matching on the word 'confidential.'
explain: EDM fingerprints real sensitive data, so it precisely detects actual records (even partial or altered) without flagging every digit string. Keyword matching is trivially evaded and noisy; blocking all uploads breaks legitimate business; and regex tuning cannot distinguish real SSNs from random digit strings.

q: Administrators currently RDP directly from their daily-use workstations to 300 servers, and one compromised admin workstation led to credential theft and lateral movement. Which architecture BEST reduces this exposure?
options: Require longer passwords for administrator accounts.
Disable RDP on all servers.
Rotate administrator passwords more frequently.
Privileged access workstations plus hardened jump (bastion) hosts: administrators authenticate to the jump host with MFA, and server credentials never touch daily-use workstations.
explain: Jump hosts with dedicated privileged workstations isolate admin sessions from the compromise-prone daily workstation, breaking the theft path. Longer or rotated passwords do not prevent credential theft from a compromised endpoint, and disabling RDP removes the administrative access the business needs.

q: For outsourced DBAs with privileged production access, management wants the ability to reconstruct exactly what commands were run during a future incident. Which control BEST provides this?
options: Privileged session recording through the PAM jump host: full keystroke and session capture of every privileged session for later replay.
Ask the DBAs to keep written notes of their activities.
Rely on database audit logs alone.
Perform an annual review of DBA access rights.
explain: Session recording captures everything executed through the privileged path in replayable form, which self-reported notes cannot reliably provide. Database logs miss OS-level actions outside the database; annual access reviews are preventive and record nothing about what was actually done.

q: Your Active Directory has domain admins logging into workstations daily, and one compromised workstation yielded DA credentials. Which model BEST contains the credential-theft blast radius?
options: Require 20-character passwords for domain admins.
Tiered administration (Tier 0/1/2): separate credentials per tier, with Tier 0 credentials never used on lower-tier systems, so a workstation compromise cannot yield domain-level credentials.
Add more domain admin accounts for redundancy.
Rename the built-in Administrator account.
explain: Tiering ensures credentials for each tier only ever touch systems at that tier, so a Tier 2 workstation compromise cannot expose Tier 0 credentials. More DAs expand the target set; renaming is obscurity (SIDs do not change); and password complexity defends against guessing, not theft from a compromised host.

q: A branch office with no secure server room and no local IT staff needs AD authentication for 50 users, but leadership fears a stolen domain controller would mean forest compromise. Which deployment fits?
options: No domain controller: authenticate every logon across the WAN.
Standalone local accounts on each branch PC.
Read-Only Domain Controller (RODC): holds no writable AD data and caches only explicitly allowed credentials, so physical theft does not expose the writable database or all domain credentials.
A standard writable domain controller in the branch office.
explain: RODCs are designed for insecure sites: read-only database, limited credential caching by policy, so theft has bounded impact. A writable DC theft is a forest-level event; WAN-only authentication fails during outages; and local accounts cannot scale or enforce central policy.

q: An attacker with brief Domain Admin access modified the AdminSDHolder container's ACL. Months later, after DA group membership was cleaned up, the attacker regained privileged access. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: The attacker never lost access because a password was never changed.
A golden ticket was forged and never expired.
The attacker compromised a domain admin account a second time through an unrelated phishing attack.

SDPROP re-applies the AdminSDHolder ACL to all protected accounts roughly every hour, propagating the backdoored ACL to privileged accounts. Audit and restore the AdminSDHolder default ACL, then hunt for its use.
explain: AdminSDHolder is the ACL template stamped by SDPROP onto protected principals (DAs, etc.) every 60 minutes, making it classic stealth persistence that survives group-membership cleanup. The fix is at the container, not the accounts. Password changes and ticket theories miss the ACL mechanism, and assuming re-compromise ignores the evidence of persistence.

q: Your fleet adds 500 Macs. You need application allowlisting and visibility into process executions on macOS without buying a commercial EDR. Which native or free controls fit?
options: Santa for binary allowlisting plus macOS Endpoint Security framework telemetry (and unified log) shipped to the SIEM for process execution visibility.
Deploy Windows Sysmon to the Macs.
Disable Gatekeeper to reduce pop-up noise for users.
Signature-based antivirus alone.
explain: Santa (Google's open-source tool) enforces binary allowlisting on macOS, and the Endpoint Security framework plus unified log provide the process telemetry a SIEM needs. Sysmon is Windows-only; disabling Gatekeeper removes a protection layer; and AV signatures alone miss living-off-the-land behavior that allowlisting and telemetry catch.

q: A US federal customer requires SBOMs in a NIST-accepted format, while your internal tooling consumes CycloneDX natively. Your build system can emit one format. Which decision is BEST?
options: Decline to provide SBOMs: they are optional documentation.
Emit CycloneDX and convert to SPDX for the customer: both formats are NTIA-recognized, converters exist, and this satisfies the federal requirement without breaking internal tooling.
Invent a compact internal JSON format that covers both needs.
Ship only the format the customer named and let internal tooling break.
explain: NTIA recognizes both SPDX and CycloneDX, and reliable converters exist, so emitting one and converting is the standard answer. A proprietary format fails the federal requirement; sacrificing internal tooling is a false choice; and SBOMs are effectively required for US federal software sales, not optional.

q: You must choose between two open-source libraries with similar features. Neither has any published CVEs. Which assessment BEST estimates their supply-chain risk before adopting one?
options: Compare GitHub star counts.
Adopt one and wait to see if a CVE is published.
OpenSSF Scorecard: automated checks of repository hygiene such as maintenance status, code review, pinned dependencies, fuzzing, and branch protection, scored per project.
Compare total download counts: the more popular library is safer.
explain: Scorecard proactively measures the security practices that predict future vulnerabilities, which is exactly what you need when no CVEs exist yet. Download counts and stars measure popularity, not hygiene; waiting for a CVE is reactive and means the vulnerable code is already in your product.

q: The assessment plan includes testers attempting tailgating, badge cloning, and after-hours building entry, with written authorization and defined boundaries. Which test type is this, and what is the MOST important safeguard?
options: Social engineering, which is illegal even with authorization.
A technical network test: physical access attempts need no authorization if no systems are touched.
Physical tests have no security value and should be removed from the plan.

Physical penetration test. The critical safeguard is written authorization (the 'get-out-of-jail-free' letter) with scope, deconfliction contacts, and rules of engagement, so testers are not mistaken for real intruders.
explain: Physical pentests validate real-world controls like badge readers and guards, and like any pentest they require written authorization plus deconfliction contacts to avoid law-enforcement or guard-force incidents. Authorized testing is legal; 'just walking in' without authorization is trespassing; and dismissing physical testing ignores a genuine attack path.

q: Before an external penetration test, you want to discover forgotten subdomains (dev, staging, legacy) that may be in scope, without sending any packets to the target. Which OSINT technique is MOST appropriate?
options: Passive subdomain enumeration via certificate transparency logs, passive DNS databases, and search engines: reveals subdomains with zero target contact.
Port-scan the company's entire /16 to find web servers.
Ask employees which subdomains they remember.
Attempt DNS zone transfers against the authoritative servers.
explain: CT logs and passive DNS expose subdomains passively and comprehensively, which is the correct pre-engagement OSINT step. Port-scanning a /16 is active, noisy, and may exceed authorization; employee memory is incomplete; and zone transfers are almost universally refused.

q: A penetration test targets a gRPC API. The team finds the reflection service enabled in production and uses it to enumerate every method and message type. What is the finding, and what is the fix?
options: Enabling TLS on the gRPC endpoint fully remediates the finding.

gRPC server reflection exposes the full API surface in production (the gRPC equivalent of GraphQL introspection). Disable reflection in production and enforce authentication and authorization on every method.
gRPC APIs cannot be tested, so remove the API from scope.
Reflection is required for client applications to function, so it must stay enabled.
explain: Reflection is a debugging aid that discloses the entire API surface to anyone who can connect; it must be off in production with per-method authN/authZ. gRPC is testable with tools like grpcurl; clients do not need reflection; and TLS protects transport only, not API discovery.

q: A scan flags session cookies missing the Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes. Which risk does EACH missing flag create?
options: Serving the site over HTTPS alone compensates for all three missing flags.
Only the Secure flag matters; the other two are informational.

Missing Secure: the cookie is sent over unencrypted HTTP and can be stolen on the network. Missing HttpOnly: JavaScript can read the cookie, enabling theft via XSS. Missing SameSite: the browser sends the cookie cross-site, enabling CSRF.
The flags are cosmetic: modern browsers enforce equivalent protections automatically.
explain: Each flag mitigates a distinct vector: Secure enforces HTTPS-only transmission, HttpOnly blocks JavaScript access, SameSite restricts cross-site sending. Browsers do not auto-apply these; HTTPS does not stop XSS cookie theft or cross-site request forgery; and treating two of the three as informational leaves real attack paths open.

q: A penetration test shows the profile-photo upload accepts .php files, stores them in the web root, and returns the file's URL. The tester uploads a web shell and executes commands. What are the correct layered fixes?
options: Add a client-side JavaScript check that rejects .php extensions.
Block the .php extension specifically in the upload handler.
Increase the maximum upload file size so legitimate photos are not rejected.
Validate file type server-side (allowlisted extensions plus content/MIME sniffing), store uploads outside the web root or serve them non-executable, randomize filenames, and scan uploads for malware.
explain: Unrestricted upload is fixed in depth: server-side allowlist validation, safe storage outside the web root, non-executable serving, and randomized names. Client-side checks are trivially bypassed with a proxy; blocking one extension invites bypasses (.phtml, double extensions, case tricks); upload size is irrelevant to the vulnerability.

q: An attacker requests /account/settings/avatar.css, a nonexistent static path that the application maps to the authenticated account page. The CDN caches the response containing the victim's personal data under that URL, and the attacker retrieves it. What is this attack?
options: Web cache deception: the attacker tricks the cache into storing sensitive dynamic content under an attacker-chosen static-looking URL. Fix by never caching authenticated responses, normalizing cache keys, and stripping sensitive data from cacheable responses.
Web cache poisoning: the attacker injected malicious content into the cache.
Server-side request forgery (SSRF).
Session fixation.
explain: Cache deception steals private content by getting the cache to store a victim's page under the attacker's URL; the fix is cache-control discipline for authenticated content. Cache poisoning is the inverse (attacker content served to victims); SSRF involves the server making attacker-chosen requests; session fixation targets session IDs, none of which describe this.

q: A penetration test shows the checkout POST includes {'total': 199.99} and the server trusts it: changing the value to 1.99 completes the purchase at $1.99. What is the vulnerability class, and what is the fix?
options: Add client-side JavaScript validation of the total field.
Business logic flaw (client-side trust): the server must recompute prices from authoritative server-side data and never trust client-submitted totals.
SQL injection in the checkout handler.
Cross-site scripting in the cart page.
explain: Trusting client-supplied business values is a business-logic flaw; the server must be the authority on pricing. There is no database injection or script injection here, and client-side validation is bypassed in seconds with a proxy, so it is not a fix.

q: Your password policy still requires 90-day rotation and 3-of-4 character complexity. Users cope by writing passwords on sticky notes. What does NIST SP 800-63B recommend instead?
options: Add stricter complexity requirements, such as 4-of-4 character classes.
Require SMS one-time codes for all logins.
Require minimum length (8+, encourage passphrases), screen new passwords against known-breached lists, drop periodic rotation absent compromise, and drop composition rules.
Rotate passwords more frequently, such as every 30 days.
explain: SP 800-63B favors length over complexity, breached-password screening, and no arbitrary expiry, because rotation and composition rules demonstrably drive sticky-note behavior. Shorter rotation and more complexity worsen the underlying problem, and 800-63B actually restricts (not recommends) SMS as an authenticator.

q: A Linux hardening scan flags /usr/bin/vim.basic as SUID root, a nonstandard configuration. Why is this a critical finding?
options: SUID on editors is standard and expected on all Linux systems.
File permission bits do not affect privilege in practice.
Only the root user can execute SUID binaries.
Any user can run vim as root and escape to a root shell (for example, :!/bin/sh), giving instant privilege escalation. Remove the SUID bit and use sudo with least privilege instead.
explain: SUID root on a binary with shell escapes is immediate root for any local user; editors have no legitimate need for SUID. SUID is not normal for editors, permission bits are precisely what grant the elevated privilege, and any user may execute a SUID binary (that is the danger).

q: A Windows assessment finds a service with ImagePath C:\Program Files\MyApp\app.exe (unquoted) running as SYSTEM, and a standard user can write to C:\Program Files\MyApp. What is the exploit, and what is the fix?
options: Unquoted service path: Windows tries C:\Program.exe and C:\Program Files\MyApp.exe before the real path, so an attacker-planted binary runs as SYSTEM. Quote the path and fix the directory ACLs.
Reinstall the application to fix the vulnerability.
Change the service to run as Administrator instead of SYSTEM.
No issue: spaces in paths are normal and Windows handles them safely.
explain: Windows resolves unquoted paths greedily, so a writable parent directory plus an unquoted SYSTEM service equals privilege escalation; quoting and ACLs are the fix. Reinstalling preserves the flaw, switching accounts misunderstands the issue (SYSTEM is already highest), and unquoted spaces are exactly the vulnerability.

q: A scan flags AlwaysInstallElevated=1 set in both the HKLM and HKCU policy keys. Why is this rated critical?
options: Only one of the two registry keys matters, so the finding is a false positive.
Any standard user can install a crafted MSI package that executes with SYSTEM privileges: a trivial, well-known privilege escalation. Disable the policy.
It only affects users who are already administrators.
MSI packages are inherently safe and cannot execute attacker code.
explain: With both keys set, Windows Installer elevates any user's MSI to SYSTEM, a classic privesc primitive. It affects standard users, MSIs execute arbitrary code by design, and the exploit specifically requires both keys, so the pair is the true finding.

q: An assessment finds WPAD enabled via DHCP/DNS on all workstations, and the network publishes no legitimate WPAD entry, so an attacker could register one. What is the risk, and what is the fix?
options: There is no risk if the organization does not use a proxy server.
The perimeter firewall already blocks WPAD abuse.

An attacker on the LAN can serve a malicious wpad.dat proxy auto-config file, silently redirecting workstation traffic through an attacker proxy for interception. Disable WPAD where unused, or publish and harden a legitimate entry.
WPAD is required for any internet access, so it must stay enabled.
explain: WPAD auto-discovery lets any LAN attacker become the proxy via a rogue PAC file, intercepting traffic regardless of whether you use a proxy. It is only needed for proxy auto-configuration, not internet access generally; and firewalls do not inspect DHCP/DNS-based PAC discovery.

q: A scan finds Redis listening on 0.0.0.0:6379 with no authentication, reachable from the corporate LAN. Why is this critical?
options: Redis is in-memory only, so there is no data at risk.
Only database administrators can connect to Redis.
It is only a cache, so command execution is not possible.
Unauthenticated Redis allows arbitrary command execution (via CONFIG and module loading) plus full data theft. Bind it to localhost, require AUTH with a strong password, and firewall the port.
explain: Redis without authentication has well-documented remote code execution primitives (module load, config rewrite) alongside complete data access. 'In-memory' does not mean safe or non-persistent, anyone on the LAN can connect without auth, and caches holding sessions or tokens are high-value targets.

q: An assessment finds /manager/html on an internet-facing Tomcat server using admin/tomcat credentials. Why is this effectively remote code execution?
options: The Tomcat Manager application allows authenticated users to deploy WAR files, so an attacker with the default credentials deploys a malicious WAR and gains code execution. Remove the manager app or restrict it with strong credentials and IP controls.
The manager page is only a read-only status dashboard.
Default credentials on an admin page are a low-severity informational finding.
Tomcat is a static file server and cannot execute deployed code.
explain: Manager = deploy arbitrary WARs = RCE, and admin/tomcat is a universally known default on an internet-facing host. It is not read-only, default creds on a deployment interface are critical, and Tomcat is a servlet container that executes exactly what is deployed to it.

q: Your network vulnerability scans keep missing hosts behind the VPN concentrator and cannot assess configuration issues such as missing EDR agents. Which scan type fills these gaps, and what is the tradeoff?
options: Disable the VPN concentrator during scan windows.
Agent-based scanning: the agent assesses the host locally regardless of network location and reports deep configuration state. The tradeoff is agent deployment, maintenance, and lifecycle overhead.
Run the network scans more frequently.
Replace vulnerability scans with ping sweeps.
explain: Agents assess locally, so network position is irrelevant and configuration checks (EDR presence, patch state) are native; the cost is managing the agent fleet. More frequent network scans still cannot reach through the VPN or see host config, ping sweeps are discovery-only, and disabling VPN infrastructure for scanning is operationally absurd.

q: An OT assessment references the Purdue model to scope the vulnerability assessment. What does the model provide?
options: An automated patching tool for industrial firmware.
A model that applies only to enterprise IT networks.

A layered reference architecture for industrial systems (Levels 0 through 5, from physical process to enterprise), with a DMZ between IT and OT, used to scope which layers and segmentation boundaries to assess.
A vulnerability scanner designed for PLCs.
explain: The Purdue model is the standard OT architecture reference: its levels and the IT/OT DMZ define assessment scope and segmentation expectations. It is not a scanner or patching tool, and it exists specifically for industrial environments, not generic IT.

q: The plant needs historian data flowing from OT to IT, but nothing must ever flow back into the OT network. Which control enforces this physically?
options: Firewall rules allowing only outbound connections.
An air gap bridged by USB sticks carried between networks.
VLAN separation between OT and IT.
A data diode (unidirectional gateway): hardware-enforced one-way data transfer that makes return traffic physically impossible.
explain: Data diodes enforce unidirectionality at the physical layer, which software cannot misconfigure away. Firewall rules are reconfigurable and bidirectional-capable, sneakernet USBs are manual and a classic malware vector, and VLANs are logical separation that a misconfiguration or VLAN hop defeats.

q: A penetration test demonstrates breaking out of a guest VM to execute code on the hypervisor host, affecting every tenant VM on that host. Why is this rated critical beyond a single-host compromise?
options: VM escape breaks the isolation boundary: hypervisor compromise exposes all guest VMs and their data. Patch the hypervisor, harden its configuration, and segment its management interfaces.
It is equivalent to compromising a single guest VM.
It only affects the one VM the tester started from.
VM escape is theoretical and has never been observed.
explain: Escape crosses the fundamental trust boundary, multiplying impact across all tenants on the host, which is why it rates critical. It is categorically worse than a guest compromise, affects every co-hosted VM, and real hypervisor CVEs make it a demonstrated (not theoretical) risk.

q: An assessment finds a wildcard certificate (*.company.com) whose private key is installed on 40 servers, including a low-security marketing server. What is the risk?
options: Wildcard certificates cannot be abused for phishing.

One compromised key can impersonate ANY subdomain for phishing or man-in-the-middle attacks, and every additional host holding the key widens the exposure. Use per-host certificates with automated issuance instead.
Wildcard certificates are always safe to share widely.
Only the marketing website is at risk if its server is compromised.
explain: A wildcard private key is valid for every subdomain, so its compromise anywhere enables convincing phishing and interception everywhere. Sharing it to 40 hosts (including low-security ones) maximizes the theft surface; per-host automated certificates contain the blast radius.

q: Certificate renewals are manual, undocumented, and caused last quarter's outage when a public cert expired. Which approach BEST prevents recurrence?
options: Track expirations in a shared spreadsheet.
Deploy a wildcard certificate so there is only one expiration to watch.
ACME-based automation (for example, an internal ACME CA or Let's Encrypt): certificates are issued and renewed automatically, with monitoring and alerting on automation failures.
Buy longer-lived certificates to renew less often.
explain: Automation removes the human-error failure mode entirely, and monitoring catches automation failures before expiry. Longer validity only postpones the manual failure, spreadsheets are manual and error-prone, and a wildcard still expires and concentrates risk.

q: Leadership asks what 'zero trust' actually changes versus the current VPN-and-perimeter model. What is the core principle, per NIST SP 800-207?
options: Buy a stronger next-generation perimeter firewall.
Eliminate all remote access.
Keep trusting the internal LAN but add more monitoring.
Never trust, always verify: no implicit trust based on network location. Every access is authenticated, authorized, and continuously validated under least privilege, assuming breach.
explain: SP 800-207 defines zero trust as removing implicit trust zones: each transaction is verified regardless of where the requester sits. It is an architecture, not a firewall upgrade; it enables secure remote access rather than eliminating it; and continuing to trust the LAN is precisely the model it replaces.

q: A worm spread laterally across the flat server VLAN in minutes. Which control BEST limits the next worm's lateral movement?
options: Microsegmentation: granular segments with least-privilege east-west policy, so the worm is contained to its originating segment instead of reaching the whole VLAN.
Faster antivirus signature updates.
Create more VLANs without access policies between them.
Disconnect the servers from the network.
explain: Microsegmentation applies least privilege to east-west traffic, containing lateral spread by design. Antivirus is reactive once the worm moves; VLANs without policy are just labels that do not block traffic; and disconnecting servers destroys the business function they exist for.

q: An audit finds 200 users with access to systems they have not used in a year, including three departed contractors. Which process BEST prevents this accumulation?
options: Trust managers to informally report when access is no longer needed.
Periodic access recertification: system and data owners attest or revoke each user's access on a schedule, integrated with joiner-mover-leaver processes.
Require annual password changes for all users.
Assign more administrators to manage access.
explain: Recertification forces regular, owner-driven justification of every entitlement, catching drift and stale contractor access. Password changes do not revoke access, more admins expand the problem, and informal manager reports are the undocumented process that produced the current accumulation.

q: An attacker deleted their tools and cleared Prefetch on a Windows host. You still need to prove the malware executed there. Which artifact can show execution, and why does it survive?
options: Browser history: it logs every executed binary.
Nothing survives: once Prefetch is cleared and files are deleted, execution cannot be proven.
Shimcache (AppCompatCache): records executables that ran on the system, stored in the SYSTEM registry hive, so deleting Prefetch and the files does not remove it. Parse it with a forensic tool.
The Recycle Bin: it records which programs were executed.
explain: Shimcache tracks execution in the registry (SYSTEM hive), independent of Prefetch and the files themselves, so it survives both deletions. The Recycle Bin records deleted files, not execution; browser history is irrelevant to binary execution; and multiple artifacts (Shimcache, Amcache, BAM/DAM) persist beyond Prefetch.

q: A suspect in a data-theft case claims they never opened the stolen spreadsheet, which sat on a shared drive. On the suspect's workstation, the investigator parses the AutomaticDestinations folder and finds entries naming that exact spreadsheet with timestamps from last Tuesday. Which artifact did the investigator use, and what does it establish?
options: Prefetch: it proves the spreadsheet itself was opened.
The Master File Table: it records which user opened each file.
Thumbcache: it proves the file was opened by this user.
Jump Lists: per-application records of files opened through the taskbar and File Explorer, establishing that the user interacted with the spreadsheet despite the denial.
explain: AutomaticDestinations files are Jump Lists, which record user-opened files per application and directly contradict the suspect's denial. Prefetch records application execution, not document-level opens; the MFT records existence and metadata, not user interaction; thumbcache holds image thumbnails, not proof of who opened a spreadsheet.

q: A suspect deleted incriminating files and emptied the Recycle Bin. Which artifact can still identify the original file names, paths, and deletion times?
options: $I files in $Recycle.Bin: each stores the original path, size, and deletion timestamp as metadata, and they often persist after emptying until overwritten. Parse or carve them.
$R files: they store the deletion metadata.
Nothing: emptying the Recycle Bin destroys all traces of the files.
The MFT alone: it is the only artifact that records deletions.
explain: In $Recycle.Bin, $I files hold the metadata (original name, path, deletion time) while $R files hold the content; both can survive emptying until overwritten. $R files are data, not metadata; 'nothing survives' ignores recoverable $I records; and while the MFT helps, the $I file is the direct, purpose-built source for deletion metadata.

q: During triage you see Security log Event ID 1102 on a server ('The audit log was cleared') at 3 AM, initiated by an unfamiliar account. What does this indicate, and what is the immediate implication?
options: The logs are gone, so the investigation cannot proceed.
Likely anti-forensics: someone deliberately cleared the Security log. Treat it as a compromise indicator and pivot to centrally forwarded or SIEM copies of the logs plus other evidence sources.
Routine log maintenance by the backup administrator.
Normal log rotation: Windows logs 1102 every time a log rotates.
explain: Event ID 1102 records explicit clearing of the audit log, a classic anti-forensics step, especially at 3 AM by an unknown account. Log rotation does not generate 1102; and the correct move is pivoting to forwarded/SIEM copies and alternate sources, not abandoning the investigation.

q: Hunting for persistence, you query domain controllers for Event ID 4720. What does this event show, and why is it valuable?
options: Password changes on user accounts.
Successful interactive logons.
User account creation: it records when the account was created, its name, and which account created it, catching attacker-created backdoor accounts.
User account deletion.
explain: Event ID 4720 is 'a user account was created,' the direct record of backdoor account provisioning with attribution to the creator. Deletion is 4726, password changes are 4724, and logons are 4624/4625; knowing these IDs is core to AD hunting.

q: You deployed Sysmon for better endpoint visibility. Which Sysmon Event ID records network connections with the responsible process, source and destination addresses, and ports, and why is it valuable for IR?
options: Event ID 1: it records network connections.
Event ID 11: it records network connections.
Event ID 7: it records network connections.
Event ID 3 (NetworkConnect): ties every TCP/UDP connection to its originating process, revealing C2 beaconing and data exfiltration per-process during scoping.
explain: Sysmon Event ID 3 logs each network connection with full process attribution, which is how you map C2 to the responsible binary. Event ID 1 is process creation, 11 is file creation, and 7 is image/DLL loading; each answers a different investigative question.

q: An attacker is using DNS tunneling, but the host's DNS resolver logs are unavailable. Which Sysmon event can still reveal the malicious queries, and why?
options: Event ID 22 (DnsQuery): Sysmon logs DNS queries at the endpoint with the requesting process, independent of resolver or network logging.
Event ID 1: it includes DNS query names.
Event ID 3: it records the queried domain names.
Firewall logs: they always record full DNS query contents.
explain: Sysmon Event ID 22 captures DNS query names per process on the endpoint itself, surviving the loss of resolver logs. Event ID 1 covers process creation only, Event ID 3 logs connections (IPs/ports, not query names), and firewall logs frequently lack DNS payload detail.

q: Script Block Logging (Event 4104) shows heavily obfuscated commands, but you need to see which cmdlets and modules the attacker actually invoked. Which logging should have been enabled, and what does it add?
options: Disable PowerShell with AppLocker instead of logging it.
PowerShell Module Logging (Event 4103): logs pipeline execution details per module and cmdlet invocation, complementing 4104's script text with what actually executed.
PowerShell transcription only: it captures cmdlet invocation detail.
Event 4104 alone is sufficient for full reconstruction.
explain: Module Logging (4103) records cmdlet and pipeline invocation details that Script Block Logging (4104) does not, together reconstructing obfuscated activity. Transcription captures console I/O, not cmdlet-level detail; 4104 alone shows script text without invocation context; and disabling PowerShell breaks administration without answering the forensic question.

q: A suspect laptop was hibernated (not shut down) before seizure, and memory was never captured live. Which file may still contain memory contents, and what is the caveat?
options: Nothing: hibernation wipes RAM before writing to disk.
Prefetch: it preserves full memory images.
hiberfil.sys: hibernation writes RAM contents to disk, so it may hold credentials, process data, and network state. Caveat: it is compressed, may be partial, and BitLocker can encrypt it.
pagefile.sys: it is the only file that preserves hibernated memory.
explain: Hibernation persists RAM to hiberfil.sys, making it analyzable like a memory image with caveats around compression, completeness, and encryption. The pagefile is a different artifact (paging, not hibernation); hibernation preserves rather than wipes RAM; Prefetch records execution, not memory contents.

q: The company receives an email threatening a massive DDoS attack unless 10 Bitcoin is paid. No attack has occurred yet. What is this, and what is the BEST response?
options: Pay the Bitcoin immediately to prevent the attack.
Ignore it completely: no attack means no action is needed.
Shut down the public website preemptively until the threat passes.
Ransom DDoS (RDDoS) extortion: do not pay. Verify DDoS resilience (scrubbing service, CDN, rate limiting), preserve the threat message as evidence, and consider notifying law enforcement.
explain: RDDoS is pay-or-we-attack extortion; paying funds criminals with no guarantee, while the correct response is hardening defenses and preserving evidence. Ignoring it wastes the warning window to verify mitigation, and preemptive shutdown is a self-inflicted outage, which is exactly what the extortionist wants.

q: Customers report card fraud after purchases on your checkout page. The page source is unchanged, but a third-party analytics script now loads an extra obfuscated script that skims form fields. What is this attack, and what is the immediate IR step?
options: Magecart (web skimmer) via compromised third-party script: remove or revert the malicious script, rotate exposed keys, notify affected customers, and deploy Content Security Policy with subresource integrity.
SQL injection against the orders database.
A server compromise: rebuild the web server from gold images.
Customer endpoint malware: advise customers to run antivirus.
explain: Magecart skimmers harvest payment data through JavaScript, frequently via compromised third-party supply chain scripts; response targets the script supply chain plus CSP/SRI. There is no database injection here, the server itself is not compromised (the third party is), and the skimming happens server-side in the page, not on customer endpoints.

q: Search results show your corporate site ranking for pharmaceutical spam pages you never created. The CMS is unpatched and unknown administrator accounts exist. What happened, and what is the response?
options: Simply delete the spam pages and close the ticket.

SEO spam injection (parasite hosting): attackers abuse the site's domain authority for spam rankings. Remove the spam, close the access vector, reset credentials, remove rogue accounts, and request search-engine re-review.
The marketing team launched an unauthorized campaign.
DNS hijacking: the domain now resolves to the attacker's server.
explain: Attackers inject spam into high-authority sites to leech rankings; full response requires eradicating their access (unpatched CMS, rogue admins), not just deleting pages. Marketing did not do this, DNS still points to your server (which serves the spam), and page deletion alone leaves the persistence intact.

q: A breach exposed 50,000 cardholder records. The acquiring bank demands an independent investigation. Which type of firm is required, and why can't the internal team do it?
options: The internal security team: they know the environment best.
Local law enforcement: they handle all breach investigations.
A PCI Forensic Investigator (PFI): a PCI SSC-qualified firm required by card-brand rules for cardholder data breaches, because independence from the breached entity is mandated.
Any general IT consulting firm.
explain: Card-brand rules require a PFI (PCI SSC-qualified) for cardholder data compromises; internal teams lack the mandated independence regardless of skill. A general consultancy lacks the qualification, and law enforcement pursues criminals rather than performing the PCI-mandated forensic investigation.

q: Attribution analysis finds the malware contains Russian-language strings and Moscow compile timestamps, but the C2 infrastructure and operator working hours align with another region, and the strings appear only in non-functional comments. What should the analyst conclude?
options: The attackers are definitely Russian: the strings prove it.
Language strings are meaningless, so disregard all evidence.
Attribute the attack to the other region based on working hours alone.
Possible false flag: treat language artifacts skeptically, weight infrastructure and behavioral evidence more heavily, and do not assert attribution from strings alone.
explain: False flags are a known deception tactic and language strings are cheap to plant, so attribution must rest on harder-to-fake evidence like infrastructure and behavior. Asserting from strings alone repeats the trap; discarding everything abandons the analysis; and working hours alone are equally thin evidence.

q: During a significant cyber incident affecting critical infrastructure, beyond the FBI, which US agency should be notified for coordinated defense support, and why?
options: CISA: the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity, which shares threat intel and provides defensive assistance (it is not a law enforcement agency).
Only the FBI needs to be involved.
The FCC: it regulates cybersecurity incidents.
No other agency: additional notifications only create confusion.
explain: CISA coordinates national cyber defense and assists victims with intel and technical support, complementing the FBI's law-enforcement role. The FCC regulates communications, not incident response; and skipping CISA forfeits coordinated defense support the agency exists to provide.

q: Your team has run tabletop and functional exercises. Leadership wants the most realistic test: actual systems, real tools, a simulated adversary, under time pressure. Which exercise type is this?
options: A checklist review of the incident response plan.
Full-scale exercise: the most realistic tier, deploying actual capabilities against a live scenario; resource-intensive but the truest test of execution under pressure.
Another discussion-based tabletop exercise.
A functional exercise: it is the most realistic option available.
explain: Exercises progress tabletop (discussion) to functional (coordination validation) to full-scale (real systems, real adversary simulation), with realism and cost increasing at each tier. Another tabletop adds no realism, functional exercises stop short of full execution, and a checklist review is not an exercise at all.

q: A compromised EC2 instance is traced to an unpatched guest OS. The cloud provider says guest patching is the customer's job; your team assumed the provider handled it. What principle resolves this, and who was right?
options: The customer is responsible for everything, including the hypervisor.
Responsibility depends entirely on the specific contract wording.

The shared responsibility model: the provider secures the cloud itself (physical, hypervisor), while the customer secures what is in the cloud (guest OS, data, configurations). The provider was right about guest patching.
The provider is responsible for everything, including guest operating systems.
explain: Shared responsibility is the standard model ('of' vs. 'in' the cloud): guest OS patching is always the customer's duty in IaaS. The provider does not own guest patching, the customer does not own the hypervisor, and while contracts matter, the model itself assigns these duties by default.

q: A Google Cloud Compute Engine instance is compromised. There is no CloudTrail in this environment. Which GCP sources provide the equivalent API audit trail, and how do you preserve the disk forensically?
options: GCP has no API logging capability.
Delete the instance immediately to stop the bleeding, then investigate.
Use AWS CloudTrail: it works across clouds.
Cloud Audit Logs (Admin Activity and Data Access) provide the API trail; create a snapshot of the boot disk to preserve a forensic copy before remediation.
explain: GCP's Cloud Audit Logs are the CloudTrail equivalent, and disk snapshots are the cloud-native forensic image. GCP logging is extensive, deleting the instance destroys evidence, and CloudTrail is AWS-only.

q: Legal needs all emails of three custodians preserved for a breach lawsuit, but the 30-day retention policy auto-deletes old mail. What is the FIRST technical step?
options: Place the custodians' mailboxes on eDiscovery (litigation) hold: this immediately suspends automatic deletion for those mailboxes.
Export PST files of the mailboxes first, then decide on holds.
Email the custodians asking them not to delete anything.
Disable the retention policy for the entire organization.
explain: The hold must come first because auto-deletion continues during any export, destroying evidence while you work. User requests are unreliable and do not stop automated policy, and disabling retention org-wide is overbroad and can create spoliation issues elsewhere.

q: Eradication is declared complete after a month-long intrusion. Before closing the incident, what proactive step BEST ensures no attacker foothold remains?
options: Wait for the SIEM to alert if anything was missed.
Conduct a targeted threat hunt for the actor's TTPs and IOCs across the estate: assume breach and verify absence rather than assuming success.
Close the incident: the eradication checklist was completed thoroughly.
Reimage every host in the environment a second time.
explain: Post-incident hunting for the specific actor's techniques validates eradication instead of assuming it. Checklists can miss persistence, blind reimaging is costly without confirming scope, and passive waiting cedes the initiative to any residual foothold.

q: HR will terminate a system administrator suspected of data theft today at 5 PM. Security is asked for the technical termination checklist. What is the correct sequence?
options: Let HR handle the termination; security has no technical role.
Confront the employee about the suspicion before taking any technical action.

Preserve evidence FIRST (forensic images and logs under litigation hold), then at termination time: disable accounts, revoke certificates/tokens/VPN access, collect devices, and rotate shared credentials, synchronized minute-by-minute with HR and legal.
Delete the administrator's accounts immediately, right now.
explain: Evidence preservation must precede any action that alerts the suspect, and the technical steps must execute simultaneously with HR's notification to prevent sabotage. Early deletion destroys evidence and tips off the suspect, HR cannot perform technical revocations, and confrontation invites spoliation.

q: Investigation shows the breach came through your vendor's subcontractor, a company you have no contract with. What is this risk called, and what is the durable fix?
options: It is solely the vendor's problem: take no action.
Sue the subcontractor directly for the breach.
Terminate the vendor contract immediately regardless of business impact.
Fourth-party risk: extend due-diligence requirements contractually with flow-down clauses, inventory critical fourth parties, and monitor them.
explain: Fourth parties (your vendors' vendors) are a real and common breach path; the durable fix is contractual flow-down of security requirements plus visibility into the chain. It is your data that was breached so inaction is negligent, you typically lack privity to sue the subcontractor, and immediate termination may be operationally impossible.

q: The disaster recovery plan looks perfect on paper but has never been tested. During a tabletop, nobody can confirm the backups are actually restorable. What type of test is needed, and why?
options: A real failover test (parallel or full interruption): actually execute the recovery and validate RTO/RPO, because paper plans hide broken assumptions that only execution exposes.
Another discussion-based tabletop exercise.
A checklist review of the DR documentation.
Trust the backup vendor's assurances.
explain: Only executing failover proves recoverability and validates RTO/RPO; tabletops and checklists cannot confirm backups restore. Another tabletop repeats the discussion that already failed to provide assurance, and vendor assurances are not evidence.

q: During an incident, responders discover corporate email and VoIP are compromised, and nobody has anyone's personal cell number. What preparation would have prevented this scramble?
options: Coordinate over public social media direct messages.
